books.title: Phaedo
books.author: Plato
books.desc: On the day of his execution, Socrates discusses with his friends whether the soul survives death, before calmly drinking the hemlock.
about: At Phlius, Phaedo of Elis tells Echecrates about the last hours of Socrates, which he spent with him in the prison at Athens in 399 BC. Surrounded by friends, Socrates explains why a philosopher should not fear death, and discusses with the Thebans Simmias and Cebes whether the soul is immortal. He offers several arguments, drawing on the idea that learning is recollection and on the theory of Forms, and answers their objections, before ending with a myth about the fate of souls.

The dialogue is one of Plato's most important works on the soul, knowledge and the philosophical life, which Socrates describes as a preparation for death. It is also a moving portrait of Socrates' serenity in his final hours.
Plato wrote the Phaedo in the fourth century BC. This English translation is by Benjamin Jowett, the Oxford scholar whose translations of Plato's dialogues were published in the nineteenth century.

books.title: Leviathan
books.author: Thomas Hobbes
books.desc: Writing during the English Civil War, Hobbes argues that only a powerful sovereign, created by agreement among people, can save them from the war of all against all.
about: Hobbes begins with human nature: sensation, imagination, reason, the passions and the restless desire for power. Without a common power to keep them in awe, he argues, people live in a condition of war of every man against every man, in which the life of man is "solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short". To escape it, they agree to transfer their rights to a sovereign whose authority must be undivided. The book is divided into four parts: Of Man, Of Common-wealth, Of a Christian Common-wealth and Of the Kingdome of Darknesse.

Leviathan is a founding work of modern political philosophy and of social contract theory. Its account of the state of nature, natural law and absolute sovereignty, and its criticism of the political power of churches, have been debated ever since.

Leviathan, or The Matter, Forme, and Power of a Common-wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civill was printed in London for Andrew Crooke in 1651, at the end of the English Civil War. This edition keeps the spelling of the original.
books.author_short: English philosopher (1588–1679), author of Leviathan and one of the founders of modern political philosophy.
author_long: Thomas Hobbes was born on 5 April 1588 at Westport, near Malmesbury in Wiltshire. After studying at Magdalen Hall, Oxford, he became tutor to the Cavendish family, with whom he travelled in Europe, meeting figures such as Galileo and Descartes. He died at Hardwick Hall in Derbyshire on 4 December 1679.
His works include The Elements of Law (1640), De Cive (1642), Leviathan (1651), De Corpore (1655) and Behemoth, a history of the English Civil War published in 1681.

books.title: The Wild Duck
books.author: Henrik Ibsen
books.desc: An idealist determined to reveal the truth about his friend's marriage brings disaster to a poor photographer's family.
about: Gregers Werle, the son of a wealthy merchant, returns home after years away and despises his father. He finds his old school friend Hjalmar Ekdal living contentedly as a photographer with his wife Gina, their young daughter Hedvig and his father, old Ekdal, who keeps a wild duck and other animals in the garret. Convinced that his friend's happiness rests on lies about the past, and that the truth will make him free, Gregers resolves to tell Hjalmar everything, despite the warnings of Dr Relling.
Ibsen's drama, mixing comedy and tragedy, questions the demand for absolute truth and asks whether people need illusions, the "life-lie" defended by Relling, in order to live.
The Wild Duck was published in 1884 and first performed on 9 January 1885 at Den Nationale Scene in Bergen. This English translation by Eleanor Marx Aveling was published in 1890.

books.title: Kipps
books.author: H. G. Wells
books.desc: A shy draper's assistant in Folkestone unexpectedly inherits a fortune and struggles to find his place in polite society.
about: Arthur Kipps, an orphan brought up by his aunt and uncle in New Romney, is apprenticed to Mr Shalford's drapery shop in Folkestone. Long hours and petty rules leave him little hope of improvement, until the eccentric actor and would-be playwright Chitterlow shows him a newspaper advertisement that leads to a large inheritance. Suddenly rich, Kipps becomes engaged to the refined Helen Walshingham, who sets out to educate him, but he is torn between his new life and his childhood sweetheart Ann Pornick.
Wells's comic novel is an affectionate and satirical study of the English class system, social snobbery and the difficulty of crossing class boundaries.
Kipps: The Story of a Simple Soul was published in 1905.

books.title: Jo's Boys
books.author: Louisa May Alcott
books.desc: Ten years after Little Men, the boys of Plumfield have grown up and set out into the world, while Jo watches over them.
about: Plumfield, the school run by Jo and Professor Bhaer, has become a college. The boys who grew up there are now young men: Nat studies music in Germany, Emil is a sailor, the restless Dan seeks adventure in the West, Demi looks for his career, and Tommy, Ted and the others face love, work and their own mistakes. Jo, now a famous author besieged by admirers, follows each of them with affection and advice.

Alcott's final novel about the March family deals with growing up, choosing a vocation, temptation and women's education and independence. Its picture of Native Americans, seen through Dan's adventures in the West, reflects the attitudes and vocabulary of its time.

Jo's Boys, and How They Turned Out: A Sequel to "Little Men" was written between 1882 and 1886, while Alcott was suffering from chronic illness, and published in 1886. It is the last book of the series that began with Little Women.
